analysis.title: The Texas Copycats: Georgia, Ohio, Michigan Line Up For Data Center Pauses; Here's The Damage
key_insights: Goldman sees Democratic wins at the state level leading to data center moratoria that could affect about 45% of planned US data center capacity. Texas alone is roughly a quarter of that, and the other ~20% sits in other states.

Jefferies' Julien Dumoulin-Smith calls data centers 'a bipartisan affordability issue' after data center-skeptic Democrats won governorships in TX, GA, OH, NV, MI, WI and IA. He expects 'anti-data center efforts to continue across many state legislatures in 2027.'
Wolfe's Chris Senyek says Texas 'could likely serve as a model for opposition response to the buildout.'
In a Jefferies client survey taken Monday, investors called six of the eight key races correctly, but 64% expected Abbott to keep Texas. Kansas is still pending.

Georgia: Keisha Lance Bottoms won on a temporary statewide pause, and Democrats took both PSC seats, flipping the commission to 3-2 Democratic (first Democratic majority since 1995, per Jefferies). Goldman's Davenport sees the outcome as potentially negative for Southern's prospective large load pipeline of 75 GW+. Southern (SO) has 56% of its rate base in Georgia.

Ohio: Amy Acton beat Vivek Ramaswamy on a conditional moratorium that, per Jefferies, requires data centers to cover 100% of utility costs, bring their own generation, use union labor and end NDAs. Goldman expects ~8 GW online in Ohio by 2030, now facing potentially more stringent requirements. Ohio power bills are up 27%.

Michigan: Jocelyn Benson wants a moratorium until guardrails on water, power costs and local decision-making are in place. Wells Fargo's utilities team calls the result 'neutral to constructive' because she still supports 'responsible' development.

Wisconsin's Crowley committed to repealing the state's data center sales-tax exemption, and Iowa's Sand wants to eliminate Iowa's data center incentives. Kansas is too close to call (Jefferies had Holscher up 50.3% to 49.7% with 98% reporting). Arizona's Corporation Commission is also undecided, with Democrats Pratte and Hill leading on calls for a statewide moratorium.

Florida and Louisiana are the bright spots for hyperscalers. Byron Donalds held Florida (~50% to 49%), removing Jolly's proposed statewide moratorium. Republicans swept both Louisiana PSC seats to expand control to 4-1, which Wells Fargo calls 'the most constructive setup' for Entergy (ETR).
GLJ's Gordon Johnson thinks Texas projects with neither power nor permits 'probably go to Louisiana, Oklahoma or nowhere.'
A Heatmap survey cited by Jefferies shows Americans who 'strongly oppose' a data center near them rose from 24% in September 2025 to 61% in August 2026. 'Strongly support' fell from 13% to 4%.

Goldman's Davenport says the Texas outcome 'could drive negative reactions for exposed stocks including Buy rated VST, NRG, SRE, and XEL, as well as Neutral rated CEG and AEP.' The risk is to the timing of the load growth inflection, which could affect ERCOT power prices and regulated utility capex.

Wells Fargo's Pourreza calls the Texas result 'a major surprise relative to our expectation' and expects 'a negative stock reaction as investors reassess the Texas growth premium.' He also flags Hinojosa's residential rate freeze as a separate cost-recovery problem.

Jefferies says 'Laggards include anything that touches data centers': IPPs (NRG, Vistra, Talen), CenterPoint (CNP, ~80% of rate base in Texas, ~12% premium to the group), Atmos (ATO), EPCs with Texas exposure, and gas midstream on lower demand.

Jefferies' winners are 'few and far between': clean energy (Nextpower, NXT, the new Franchise Pick), NextEra (NEE) and Duke (DUK) on the Florida result, and defensive AWK, ConEd (ED) and gas LDCs. Longer term, Jefferies thinks stable-regulation Midwest and Mountain names (ETR, AEE, BKH, NWE, MDU, LNT) 'should net emerge better positioned to capture data center development.'
Early tech tape, per Bloomberg: CoreWeave, Tesla and SpaceX fell more than 5%, while Meta, Amazon and Alphabet traded higher.

Goldman's TMT desk puts Texas at 'circa. 27%' of planned capacity. It warned that Tuesday's pre-result squeeze in CIFR (+18.4%), HUT (+16%) and WULF (+14.5%) provided 'context, rather than proof that those risks have been discounted.'

Contrarian view: Goldman's Rich Privorotsky argues 'throttling the supply of compute doesn't necessarily destroy demand' and could push pricing for existing capacity higher for longer. Wells Fargo's Jerry Revich agrees 'token economics remain attractive.' Oracle reported 97.9% AI infrastructure utilization and a 20% average renewal/resale premium, H100 rental rates are up 26% y/y, and GB200 rental pricing is up 50% YTD.

Federal override looks unlikely. Goldman says federal data center rules would still need bipartisan Senate support and to overcome a veto. Jefferies says the sweep 'raises the odds of a federal ratepayer protection bill in 2027' and 'lowers the odds of a lame-duck permitting deal.' H.R. 9340 passed the House but fell three votes short of cloture in the Senate in September. This is a near-term negative for gas midstream.
Goldman expects Democrats to use the December 11 funding deadline and next fall's debt limit to 'limit the war with Iran, roll back selected tariffs, and reverse spending cuts enacted last year.'

Jefferies' summary is 'Demand moves right, not away.' It says many early indications are for pragmatic new Democratic governors, with potential announcements as soon as 1Q27 in select states. Goldman's Davenport still sees Texas and Georgia as 'important longer-term areas for load growth.'

Timing constraints on the 'moves right' thesis: the Texas session ends May 31, Georgia's commission now has a Democratic majority heading into the 2028 rate case, and the Ohio governor appoints three of five PUCO commissioners in her first term.

Capital is sorting toward states that make data centers pay their own way (Louisiana, Oklahoma, Wyoming, Florida) and toward companies that already own energized megawatts, as BofA predicted in Monday's preview.

risk_factors: Moratoria or stricter requirements in Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Michigan and other states could delay load growth and cut utility capex.
Texas rate freeze (Hinojosa's residential rate freeze) is a separate cost-recovery risk.
Public opposition is rising: 61% strongly oppose a local data center in August 2026, up from 24% in September 2025.
Federal preemption is unlikely, and a federal ratepayer protection bill in 2027 is more likely.
A lame-duck permitting deal is less likely, which hurts gas midstream.
Neoclouds with no energized capacity are exposed if projects are blocked.
Pending races (Kansas, Arizona Corporation Commission) could add more moratorium risk.

tension_points.bull_case: Jefferies says 'Demand moves right, not away,' with pragmatic new Democratic governors and possible announcements as soon as 1Q27. Goldman's Davenport still sees Texas and Georgia as important longer-term load growth areas.
tension_points.bear_case: Goldman sees moratoria affecting about 45% of planned capacity. Texas, Georgia and Ohio races flipped on affordability, Heatmap shows 61% strongly oppose a local data center, and federal preemption is unlikely.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A federal ratepayer protection bill in 2027 or Texas session action before May 31 would shift the outcome. Pragmatic governor announcements as soon as 1Q27 would support the bull case.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman's Privorotsky argues throttling compute supply doesn't destroy demand and could lift prices for existing capacity. Wells Fargo cites Oracle at 97.9% utilization, H100 rental up 26% y/y and GB200 up 50% YTD.
tension_points.bear_case: Goldman's TMT desk warns the pre-result squeeze in CIFR, HUT and WULF is context, not proof that risks are discounted. Neoclouds without energized capacity lose out.
